sections.title: The Commission and Witness of Barnabas and Paul

blocks.text: The missionary pair, accompanied by John as an assistant, sailed to Cyprus and began their witness in the synagogues of Salamis, proclaiming the word of God to Jewish audiences. This pattern of synagogue engagement grounds the mission in diaspora Jewish contexts where Paul and Barnabas repeatedly addressed Jews, God-fearers, and other community members.

The encounter with Bar-Jesus (also called Elymas) in Paphos presents a direct contest. A Jewish sorcerer and false prophet named Bar-Jesus held influence with the Roman proconsul Sergius Paulus, a man of understanding. When Sergius Paulus called for Barnabas and Saul to hear God's word, Elymas opposed them, seeking to turn the proconsul from faith. Acts narrates this as a conflict over access to the proconsul's attention and allegiance, culminating in Saul's pronouncement of temporary blindness upon Elymas.

The proconsul, witnessing what occurred, believed, astonished at the teaching about the Lord. The episode preserves the interaction between the missionary word and a Roman official's response without generalizing it as either inevitable success or as proof of apostolic authority over opponents.

Pisidian Antioch, identified through inscriptions, urban archaeology, imperial honors, and colonial title, was a significant Roman settlement in the wider Anatolian landscape. The city's civic importance and placement on the imperial road network made it a strategic point for missionary engagement.

Upon arrival at Antioch, Paul and his companions entered the synagogue on the Sabbath day. Acts describes a Sabbath gathering involving synagogue leaders, Israelites, God-worshipers, and women of standing—a mixed audience of Jewish and gentile participants. The synagogue functioned as a place of Scripture reading, teaching, communal deliberation, and response. This setting preserves the Jewish and gentile participation in diaspora synagogue life rather than depicting the synagogue as merely a failed preliminary step toward gentile mission.
